data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future truth, but as a methodological rule to maximize the severity of future tests; accepting this costs us the comfort of believing our chosen theory is likely true, restricting 'preference' to a procedural mandate for risk-taking rather than a guide to probable success.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent acts expecting the theory to succeed practically rather than expecting it to potentially fail informatively.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If corroboration is interpreted as a probability metric rather than a historical report of test severity.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference leads to dogmatic adherence rather than continued attempts to falsify the preferred theory.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Critical Preference as Test-Severity Maximization: The agent selects the theory with the highest corroboration because it has survived the most severe tests (highest informational content), making it the best target for further falsification attempts. Acting on it is not betting on its truth, but betting on its capacity to reveal error quickly if it is false.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
